questions.question: What is the primary responsibility of a Level 1 (L1) SOC Analyst?
options: Reverse-engineer zero-day exploits
Perform initial alert triage, entity identification, and escalate verified threats
Re-architect company firewalls
Conduct legal press conferences
questions.explanation: L1 analysts monitor incoming queues, verify facts (WHO, WHAT, WHERE, WHEN), and escalate confirmed incidents according to playbooks.

questions.question: Do you need prior hacking or advanced programming skills to start as an L1 analyst?
options: Yes, must know assembly language
No, keen observation, checklist discipline, and curiosity are primary
Yes, minimum 5 years in malware authoring
Only if working on Linux
questions.explanation: L1 operations emphasize disciplined triage, pattern recognition, and following Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs).

questions.question: When an alert sounds, what is the analyst’s immediate mindset?

Stay calm, verify the facts, and follow standard checklists

questions.question: Why do we inspect suspicious executable attachments inside an isolated VM?
options: VMs are faster than real hardware
To prevent accidental infection of your primary workstation or network
Because Windows cannot open files
VMs have better screen resolution
questions.explanation: Isolated virtual machines isolate hazardous payloads from production networks and enable clean resets.

chapters.title: Evidence handling and asking for help

questions.question: What is the best way to ask Mentor Ananya for help with an unfamiliar alert?
options: Say "the screen looks weird"
Provide the Alert ID, user, host, observed timeline, and specific question
Wait until your shift ends
Forward the alert to the entire company
questions.explanation: A structured question with Alert ID and observed evidence allows mentors to give quick, targeted guidance.

questions.question: What should you do before executing any unfamiliar command or payload in a lab?
options: Verify you are in an isolated VM or safe sandbox
Send it via email to test filters
Disable your firewall
Execute as Domain Admin
questions.explanation: Always verify sandbox isolation to prevent unintended execution.

chapters.title: Hardware, OS and accounts
chapters.concept: Understanding CPU, RAM, disk, OS architecture, and user accounts (standard vs administrative/root privileges).
chapters.visualDesc: Visual story: Ravi inspecting workstation resources, local accounts, and privilege levels.
chapters.interactiveDesc: Privilege Level Matcher: Distinguish standard user permissions from local admin / root capabilities.

questions.question: Why are standard office employees not given Administrator privileges by default?
options: To save RAM
To prevent accidental system corruption and limit the impact if an account is compromised
Because Windows requires it
To reduce electricity consumption
questions.explanation: Principle of Least Privilege prevents malware executing under a standard account from modifying core OS files.

chapters.title: Files, paths and permissions
chapters.concept: Windows vs Linux paths, executable extensions (.exe, .bat, .ps1, .sh), hidden files, and read/write/execute permissions.
chapters.visualDesc: Interactive path comparison: C:\Windows\System32 vs /etc and /var/log directories.
chapters.interactiveDesc: File Path Inspector: Spot anomalous executable paths like running binaries directly from C:\Users\...\AppData\Local\Temp.

questions.question: Why is an executable launching directly from a user’s Temp directory suspicious?
options: Temp directories are read-only
Standard software installs to Program Files; malware frequently drops into Temp folders
Windows deletes Temp every 5 minutes
Temp folders only contain text files
questions.explanation: Standard users have write permissions in Temp folders, making them a common staging ground for dropped payloads.

questions.question: Which Linux directory holds system configuration and service definitions?
options: /tmp
/etc
/dev
/media
questions.explanation: /etc stores system-wide configuration files.

units.title: Processes and Services
units.description: What processes and background services do, process trees, and distinguishing routine from unfamiliar activity.

chapters.title: What processes and services do
chapters.concept: Process IDs (PIDs), parent processes (PPID), and background services running independently of logged-in sessions.
chapters.visualDesc: Diagram: A legitimate process tree (explorer.exe -> winword.exe) vs an anomalous tree (winword.exe -> powershell.exe).
chapters.interactiveDesc: Process Lineage Tracing: Trace child PIDs back to their originating parent process.

questions.question: What is a PPID in operating systems?
options: Process Protection Identifier
Parent Process ID
Private Protocol Index
Password Packet Identifier
questions.explanation: PPID refers to the Process ID of the parent application that spawned the child process.

chapters.title: Routine versus unfamiliar activity
chapters.concept: Establishing host baselines: recognizing standard Windows binaries (svchost.exe, lsass.exe) vs typosquatted names (scvhost.exe).
chapters.visualDesc: Comparison chart: Legitimate system processes vs common masquerading techniques.
chapters.interactiveDesc: Anomaly Spotter: Find the imposter process name among standard system processes.

questions.question: What makes "svch0st.exe" running from C:\Users\Public highly suspicious?
options: It uses a zero instead of "o" and runs from an unusual directory
Windows does not have svchost
It is running as a service
Public folder is read-only
questions.explanation: Adversaries use typosquatting and staging directories (C:\Users\Public) to masquerade as core Windows services.

questions.question: Under normal circumstances, what process spawns user applications after logging into Windows?
options: explorer.exe
lsass.exe
smss.exe
wininit.exe
questions.explanation: Windows Explorer (explorer.exe) represents the user desktop shell and launches user-initiated applications.

questions.question: Which command quickly displays your current user account in both Windows cmd and Linux bash?
options: whoami
netstat
dir
ipconfig
questions.explanation: `whoami` prints the current username in both operating systems.

chapters.title: Users, hostnames and timestamps
chapters.concept: Correlating user account names with machine hostnames and normalizing UTC timestamps across time zones.
chapters.visualDesc: Timeline graphic: Converting local IST (+05:30) event logs into universal UTC timestamps.
chapters.interactiveDesc: Timestamp Normalizer: Match IST timestamps to standard UTC timestamps.

questions.question: Why do SOC analysts normalize timestamps across different system logs to UTC?
options: Computers can only count in UTC
To accurately reconstruct the sequence of events across servers in different time zones
UTC prevents viruses
To make logs shorter
questions.explanation: Reconstructing an intrusion timeline requires a common reference clock across all distributed endpoints and sensors.

questions.question: Which command lists active network sockets and listening ports on Windows?
options: netstat -ano
hostname
taskkill
echo
questions.explanation: `netstat -ano` displays active TCP/UDP connections and associated process IDs.

questions.question: What is the key takeaway when evaluating Preparation, detection, response and recovery in an L1 operational setting?
options: Always verify the observed evidence and correlate across multiple records
Assume the first alarm is 100% correct without checking
Delete the log entry to reduce ticket queue count
Immediately shutdown the entire branch network
questions.explanation: Careful verification and corroborating facts across sources prevents false alarms and ensures high evidence quality.

questions.question: How does understanding L1 responsibilities and escalation assist an L1 analyst on shift?
options: It allows distinguishing normal baseline operations from suspicious outliers
It guarantees zero alerts will ever trigger
It replaces the need for a SIEM
It eliminates the need for supervisor handoffs
questions.explanation: Understanding expected baseline behaviors enables analysts to quickly spot deviations and anomalous patterns.

questions.question: In Unit 1 (Incident Response Lifecycle), what is the primary standard for documenting findings?
options: Clear facts with supporting timestamps, host, and user references
Personal opinions without log evidence
One-word answers without context
Forwarding raw screenshots without explanation
questions.explanation: Professional SOC documentation requires specific facts, timestamps, and verifiable references.
